stances.claim: Their 62-year marriage was 'idyllic' despite genuine differences in upbringing, aptitudes, religiosity, and values -- turned by God's grace into complementary strengths.
stances.rhetorical_move: Opening confession of differences followed by faith-mediated synthesis -- defeats sentimental homogenization of long marriage.

stances.claim: Leni's passing was sudden, unexpected, and silent -- she was hospitalized for hypoglycemia (already arrested 12 hours earlier by 'two miniature Toblerone chocos'), cold sweat, and weakness, not for any heart condition; she had no heart history.
stances.rhetorical_move: Forensic-medical detail used to convey shock and to refute any presumption of foreseeability.

stances.claim: She did not suffer at the end -- 'she did not wrench, she did not wince, she did not balk' -- and passed 'as silently as when she worked alone, painted alone.'
stances.rhetorical_move: Triadic negative anaphora paired with biographical signature ('worked alone, painted alone') for consolation framing.

stances.claim: Grief will never go away -- must be befriended, not defeated; the consolation is that the Divine Master will love Leni 'better than I can ever, ever do.'
stances.rhetorical_move: Reframes acceptance as ongoing companionship with grief rather than its conquest.

one_paragraph_summary: Delivered on the last day of Leni's wake (Saturday, April 15, 2023) at the Santuario de San Antonio Parish Church in Makati and published two days later, this is CJ Panganiban's eulogy for his wife Elenita 'Leni' Carpio Panganiban -- and the most personally exposed piece in his published canon. He opens by naming the 62-year marriage 'idyllic' despite real differences in upbringing, aptitudes, religiosity, and values -- Leni spiritual where he was pedestrian, shy where he was outgoing, private and 'at her best when working alone, painting alone,' against his own appetite for socializing, dancing, public speaking, multitasking, writing, arguing, philosophizing -- and credits God's grace with turning differences into opportunities to grow in the Lord. As memorial framing he recounts their Diamond Wedding Anniversary one year prior in the secluded Carmelite Chapel in Tagaytay, presided over by Cardinal Jose F. Advincula Jr., attended exclusively by 86 incumbent archbishops and bishops, immediate family, Chief Justice Alexander G. Gesmundo (representing the Supreme Court), and Tessie Sy-Coson (whose family hosted the dinner at Tagaytay Highlands). The grief section, signaled by an ALL-CAPS turn ('BUT NOW MY LENI IS GONE'), recounts the sudden Easter Sunday passing -- Leni hospitalized at Makati Medical Center for hypoglycemia already arrested 12 hours earlier by 'two miniature Toblerone chocos,' cold sweat, and general weakness, not heart issues; she had jovially chit-chatted with New York City children and grandchildren the evening before, and 'none of us -- none of us -- expected My Leni to pass so fast.' The consolation hinges on absence of suffering at the end ('she did not wrench. She did not wince. She did not balk') and on the theological promise that the Divine Master will love her 'better than I can ever, ever do.' He declares himself 'drained, exhausted, depressed, shattered. But not defeated,' resolving to 'try to befriend grief for it will never go away,' and closes with the triadic farewell -- 'till we meet again, till we embrace again, till we are joyous again in the Heavenly Kingdom soon.'
